title: Mustang Identification Codes
introduction:
The VIN is the car’s identity string; the vehicle certification (VC) label is its compact factory packing slip. I use them together to connect the Mustang in front of me with its body, engine and equipment codes, instead of letting a badge do all the talking.

Start with the locator drawings, then match the characters on your car to the relevant entries. The numbered circles in the VIN drawing identify groups in its legend; they are not VIN character positions. On the VC label drawing, follow the leader lines and use printed field labels such as EXT PNT, INT TR, AXLE and TR. The X characters are placeholders, not codes to decode.

This guide explains identification and code lookup. It retains the dealer referrals for replacement labels, identifies paint finishes without teaching refinishing, and explains the check-digit discrepancy without becoming a VIN calculation tutorial. Use the entries within this Mustang reference’s stated scope.

edits.text: The VIN combines letters and numbers into a 17-character identifier. Look through the windshield at the upper left of the dash: the VIN is stamped on a metal tab riveted to the instrument panel. You can also find the VIN on the VC label. If the VIN plate needs replacement, an authorized dealer must contact its respective regional office.
edits.why: I use the windshield locator to find the plate without removing dash parts. The separate VC label provides another place to read the vehicle’s identifier; replacement of the plate requires the stated dealer referral.

edits.text: Read the first 3 VIN positions together as the WMI (world manufacturer identifier), then match that group to the entry below.
edits.why: This group identifies the manufacturer and vehicle category.

edits.text: 1FA: Ford Motor Company, USA, passenger car.
Read the fourth VIN position as the vehicle restraint type code and match it to the body-style-qualified entry below.
edits.why: The code identifies the listed restraint equipment; it does not establish that equipment’s present condition.

edits.text: 6: Coupe — active safety belts at all positions; driver and front passenger air bags; driver and front passenger knee inflatables; side inflatables for the 1st and 2nd row.
T: Convertible — active safety belts at all positions; driver and front passenger air bags; driver and front passenger knee inflatables; side inflatables for the 1st and 2nd row.
Vehicle Line, Series and Body Codes
Read positions 5 through 7 together to identify the vehicle line, series and body type.
edits.why: Treat this as a complete code group. Its ending distinguishes the listed coupe, convertible and equipment variants.

edits.text: Match the eighth VIN position to the engine entries below to identify engine type, displacement and cylinder count.
edits.why: I check this code before choosing engine-specific information. The engine letter belongs to this VIN position; the same letter elsewhere can mean something entirely different.

edits.text: F: 5.0L, DOHC, 4-valve, sequential fuel injection, V8.
edits.why: DOHC means double overhead camshaft.

edits.text: H: 2.3L Ti-VCT (twin independent variable cam timing), turbocharged, in-line 4-cylinder.
edits.why: Ti-VCT adjusts intake and exhaust camshaft timing independently while the engine runs.

edits.text: The ninth VIN position is the check digit, which helps detect errors when a VIN is copied. The primary manual calls it a “government-assigned, computer-generated check digit.” The supplied historical federal rule instead describes manufacturer calculation after the other VIN characters have been determined. It also permits X, which the manual’s range below omits. See the [supplied historical federal VIN rule](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2015-title49-vol6/pdf/CFR-2015-title49-vol6-sec565-15.pdf).
edits.why: Think of the check digit as a typo tripwire. The official context explains its purpose and reconciles the manual’s wording; it does not support treating the check digit as individually assigned by the government.

edits.text: 0-9 — the check-digit range printed in the primary manual.
edits.why: That printed range is incomplete: the linked historical federal rule also permits X. An X in this position is therefore not, by itself, evidence of an invalid VIN.

edits.text: Read the tenth VIN position as the model year code and match it to the entry below.
edits.why: The VC label’s manufacture date and the VIN’s model year are different identification fields.

edits.text: Read the eleventh VIN character as the assembly plant code.
edits.why: This identifies the assembly location represented by the entry below.

edits.text: 5: Flat Rock Assembly, Flat Rock, Michigan (USA).

Read the last 6 VIN positions together as the numeric vehicle build-sequence code. This is also the vehicle serial and warranty number. The serial number can also be found on the engine block, transmission and frame.
edits.why: The sequence distinguishes the individual vehicle within the identification scheme. The additional marking locations are identification references; this overview does not provide access instructions for those components.

edits.text: Use the side-view locator to find the VC label in the left door-opening area near the rear edge of the door. The label identifies the manufacturer, month and year of manufacture, certification statement and VIN, along with GVW and tire information. If the label needs replacement and the vehicle is 4 years old or less, an authorized dealer must submit the VIN to its respective regional office. That office submits a web form to the assembly plant for a replacement label. After printing, a regional-office representative delivers the label to the dealer and witnesses its installation on the vehicle. If the vehicle is more than 4 years old, the dealer must request the replacement label through the Department of Motor Vehicles.
edits.why: GVW means gross vehicle weight. Use the enlarged label drawing and its legend to locate individual code fields. The replacement routing is the primary manual’s stated process, including the age-dependent branch and witnessed installation.

edits.text: Read the paint identification as a 2-part code. The first set of numbers/letters identifies the primary body color; the second set, when present, identifies a 2-tone or accent body color. The manual makes the general statement that all paint codes use a base coat/clear coat finish, but its own entries explicitly identify tri-coat exceptions below. Retain those specific finish descriptions when reading the color code.
edits.why: I keep the color name and its finish description together. The general finish statement should not erase the explicitly listed tri-coat exceptions, and this code lookup does not prescribe a refinishing process.

edits.text: Read the interior trim identification as a 2-part code: the first character identifies the seat and fabric style, and the second identifies the interior trim color. Match each character to its respective list below.
edits.why: The manual calls these characters digits, but its seat-style entries include letters. I treat the code like a fabric swatch with a separate color tag: both parts matter.

edits.text: 4: Trend mini-perforated milled pebble leather seats.
L: Tutone natural grain leather seats (50th Anniversary).
Match the tape/paint stripe field on the VC label to the entries below, including the blank-field entry.
edits.why: A blank field has a defined meaning here; it is useful identification information.

edits.text: Blank: Less stripe — no stripe specified.
Read the radio code from the VC label’s R field and match it to the equipment combination below.
edits.why: AM and FM identify the broadcast bands, and CD means compact disc. Read the whole entry so the additional receiver features stay attached to the correct code.

edits.text: 1: AM / FM stereo with CD player.
2: AM / FM stereo with CD player and SDARS (Satellite Digital Audio Receiver System).
3: AM / FM stereo with CD player, SDARS (Satellite Digital Audio Receiver System) and HD (high-definition).
4: AM / FM stereo with CD player and dual tuner.
Read the VC label’s AXLE field and match its code to the gear ratio below, keeping any listed transmission qualifier with that entry.
edits.why: I match the letters before interpreting the ratio. A transmission qualifier belongs to its own entry and should not be carried over to a neighboring code.

edits.text: BB: 3.73 ratio, with manual or automatic transmission.

edits.why: This entry carries no transmission qualifier; it does not establish a transmission pairing.
These codes identify the transmission through the VC label’s TR field. The transmission field within the powertrain calibration identifier uses its own separate code system.

edits.text: I match the TR code on the vehicle certification label to the transmission descriptions below:
edits.why: Start with the field name before decoding the character. Otherwise, a perfectly good code can send you to the wrong dictionary.
Use the VC label’s SPR field with the appropriate front or rear list. These mappings identify springs; they do not specify spring rates or teach spring replacement.

edits.text: Read the spring identification as a 2-part code: the first group of characters identifies the front springs, and the second group identifies the rear springs.
edits.why: I keep the groups in their original order, like address labels for opposite ends of the car. A matching letter group only makes sense within the correct front or rear list.
Match the leading group from the SPR field to this list.
Match the trailing group from the SPR field to this list. Retain the complete identifier, including its prefix and suffix.

I use the label illustration to find the stacked calibration field below the barcode, immediately to the right of SPR, where the arrow points. The character diagram and its accompanying table then divide the identifier into named fields. The X characters are placeholders, not a sample calibration to decode. Think of this identifier as the calibration’s name tag: it distinguishes applications, but it is not a programming instruction. The revision field shown in the diagram is obtained through a scan tool rather than read from the printed label.

edits.text: NOTE: The VC label holds a maximum of 5 powertrain calibration characters per line. An identifier longer than 5 characters continues on the second line; read the upper line first, then continue with the lower line.
edits.why: The line break is a printing limit, not the end of the identifier. In the character diagram, the unique-calibration field crosses that break, so stopping at the upper line would leave it incomplete.
Here, model year means the year in which the calibration strategy was first introduced. I do not treat that field as a statement of the vehicle’s manufacture date.
This field identifies the vehicle application within the calibration identifier.

Use these entries for the transmission field in the calibration identifier. They distinguish automatic from manual applications; use the separate VC transmission-code list to identify the listed transmission model.
Similar-looking Mustangs can need different calibrations because their hardware or drive configuration differs. This field distinguishes those applications.

edits.text: The Emission/Corporate Average Fuel Economy/CO2 Compliance Department assigns these calibration numbers. They distinguish otherwise similar vehicles by tires, drive configurations, final drive ratios and other factors that affect calibration. An analyst chooses these 2 characters to make each calibration identifiable. For example, using 2 for a 2-valve engine and 4 for a 4-valve engine would make that difference easy to recognize.
edits.why: The valve example illustrates an analyst’s choice; it is not a universal decoding rule for every calibration. I preserve the assigned characters rather than trying to reverse-engineer them from the car’s equipment.

The fleet field describes the calibration’s fleet classification. Match its character to the entries below without treating the classification as a fault diagnosis or proof of how the car has been used.

edits.text: 0 — certification fleet (U.S. 4K, final sale in export markets)
2 — Fast Automobile Manufacturers' Association, U.S. fleet

edits.why: EVAP refers to evaporative emissions: the system that contains fuel vapor and manages its later use by the engine. Here it names a fleet classification, not an emissions-system fault.

edits.text: 7 — mileage accumulation, aging, endurance and durability fleet

edits.why: OBD means on-board diagnostic. Its appearance in this field identifies the fleet category, not a stored diagnostic trouble code.

This field identifies the certification region; when a calibration includes multiple regions, it identifies the lead region. I read these as the manual’s historical calibration categories, retaining its geographical names and qualifiers rather than updating them into a present-day market list.

edits.text: A — U.S. federal certification region, including altitude; may include Canada and/or Mexico
B — U.S. California-standard certification region, including U.S. green states
E — European Community certification region: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and UK (United Kingdom)
F — European Extended Community certification region: E-plus Croatia, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Norway, Poland, Romania, Russian Federation, Slovakia, Slovenia, Switzerland and Yugoslavia
G — GCC (Gulf Cooperative Council) certification region: Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE (United Arab Emirates)
Q — South America certification region: Brazil
U — South America certification region: unleaded fuel regions
X — Rest Of World certification region
Calibration Revision Level (Not Printed on Label)
edits.why: Obtain the revision level through a diagnostic scan tool with calibration-information capability, then match it to the categories below. A basic fault-code reader may lack that function. The revision level advances as revisions occur, but these categories are not a single numerical ladder. This reference identifies levels; it does not teach module programming.
